blocks.html: Welcome to the course. Before we read a single sign, we need a picture of the world that wrote them. The Aegean is the sea between mainland Greece and Anatolia (modern Turkey). To its south lies Crete, a long, mountainous island about 260 km from end to end. Between them are the Cyclades, a scatter of small islands. In the Bronze Age, from about 3000 to about 1100 BC, people here used bronze (copper mixed with tin) for tools and weapons, and the sea joined them more than it kept them apart.

blocks.cap: The Aegean: Crete to the south, the Cyclades in the middle, mainland Greece to the west and north. Each dot is a place where Bronze Age writing has been found; tap one to read about it, or switch the views.

blocks.html: The Bronze Age Aegean was not one country. It was a patchwork: a civilization on Crete, island towns in the Cyclades, and later several separate palace states on the mainland, all linked by ships.

blocks.html: Over the course you will meet three scripts from this world. Two are still unread: Cretan hieroglyphs and Linear A, used on Crete by the Minoans. The third, Linear B, was used by Greek speakers; it was deciphered in 1952, and it is the oldest written Greek we have. The map above shows where each one has been found. Notice how Linear A clusters on Crete and Linear B spreads from Knossos to the mainland palaces.

Why did the sea matter so much? Overland travel through Greece's mountains was slow, while a ship could cross from island to island, rarely out of sight of land. Goods such as copper, tin, oil, wine and fine pottery moved by sea, and so did ideas, including the idea of writing. That is how a script invented on Crete could be borrowed by people on the mainland.

Picturing "ancient Greece" as one country with one government. In the Bronze Age there was no Greek nation. Crete had its own culture and language, the islands had their own towns, and on the mainland each palace ran its own small state. Check yourself: when you read about a palace, ask which region it is in and which script its records used.

blocks.html: All the dates in this course are approximate. Bronze Age years come from pottery styles, radiocarbon and links to Egypt, and they can be off by decades. You will learn how in Dating the Aegean Bronze Age. For now, keep three anchors: writing begins on Crete around 2000 BC; Linear B appears around 1450 BC; and the palaces fall around 1200 BC.

blocks.title: Which region?
blocks.q: Pylos is a palace site with Linear B tablets. Is it on Crete, in the Cyclades, or on the mainland?
steps: Find Pylos on the map: it is on the west coast of the Peloponnese, the large southern peninsula of mainland Greece.
So Pylos is on the mainland, and its records are in Linear B, the script of the Greek-speaking palaces.

blocks.title: Island or mainland?
blocks.q: Akrotiri is a town where a few Linear A inscriptions were found. Where is it?
steps: Akrotiri is on Thera (Santorini), an island of the southern Cyclades, north of Crete.
Linear A finds on the islands show the reach of Minoan Crete.
blocks.a: On an island, Thera, in the Cyclades.

blocks.html: Next you will meet the people of Crete in The Minoans of Crete and the mainland Greeks in The Mycenaeans.

In The Aegean World you saw that Crete had its own Bronze Age civilization. Its towns, palaces, paintings and writing flourished from about 3000 BC, with the palace age from about 1900 to about 1450 BC. We call these people the Minoans. But that is not their name.

"Minoan" is a modern label. Arthur Evans, who dug at Knossos from 1900, named the civilization after Minos, a king of Crete in later Greek legend. What the people called themselves, and what language they spoke, we do not know.

Greek myths told of King Minos of Knossos, his labyrinth and the Minotaur. These stories were written down many centuries after the palaces had fallen. When Evans uncovered a huge, maze-like building at Knossos, he borrowed the king's name for the whole culture. The label stuck, and archaeologists still use it, the way we say "Bronze Age" for a time no one then called by that name.

Thinking "Minoan" is what the people called themselves, or that Minos was a real, known king. Minos belongs to legend; no inscription names him. The Minoans' own name for themselves is lost, because their script, Linear A, cannot be read. A quick check: if a sentence says "the Minoans called themselves…", it is claiming something no one knows.

items: They built large palaces around open central courts, at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros (see Knossos and the Cretan Palaces).
They painted lively frescoes, made fine pottery and carved seals, and traded across the sea with the islands, the mainland, Cyprus and Egypt.
They wrote: first Cretan hieroglyphs, mostly on seals, then Linear A on clay tablets and on stone offering tables.
Their language was not Greek, as far as anyone can tell; it matches no known language.

blocks.html: Why can we say so much about people whose writing we cannot read? Because archaeology does not need words. Buildings, pottery, tools, bones and paintings tell how people lived, built, traded and worshiped. What we lose without their words is their names, their beliefs in their own terms and their history as they told it.

Around 1450 BC many sites on Crete were destroyed. Afterward Knossos was run by Greek speakers who kept their records in Linear B, a script adapted from Linear A. That is why the Minoans' story continues in this course with The Mycenaeans.

blocks.title: Spot the label
blocks.q: Which of these words was chosen by a modern archaeologist: Knossos, Minoan, Crete?
steps: Knossos and Crete are ancient Greek place names (Knossos is even written ko-no-so in Linear B).
Minoan was coined by Evans from the legend of Minos.

blocks.html: The Minoans of The Minoans of Crete built great complexes that archaeologists call palaces. At Knossos, near modern Heraklion, the palace had hundreds of rooms on several floors. Phaistos and Malia were nearly as grand, and Zakros sat at the far eastern tip of the island.

blocks.cap: The palace sites of Crete, with Hagia Triada near Phaistos and Chania in the west. Tap a site to read about it.

blocks.html: A Cretan "palace" was far more than a royal home. Built around a central court, it was a storehouse, a workshop, a shrine and an office where records were kept: the heart of a region's economy.

What it shows

Oil, wine and grain collected and stored
Workshops for pottery, stone vessels and fine metalwork
Clay tablets, sealings and labels with writing
Officials counting what came in and went out
A gathering place, perhaps for ceremonies
blocks.cap: Clues to what the palaces were for.

blocks.html: We do not even know whether a king lived at Knossos. The word "palace" is a convenient label from Evans's time. What the buildings clearly did was gather the produce of the countryside, keep track of it and pay it out again to workers, craftsmen and gods. That is exactly the kind of business that needs writing.

Why did palaces need writing? A storeroom manager can remember a few jars. A palace with hundreds of jars, flocks across a whole region and dozens of workers cannot. Clay tablets let officials record who owed what and who had been paid. Writing in the Aegean was born as bookkeeping, and nearly everything we have from Linear A and Linear B is accounts.

Imagining a palace as only a royal residence, like a modern king's palace. The Aegean palaces were economic and religious centers first. Check yourself by asking what was found in a room: a storeroom of jars, a workshop or an archive tells you more about the building than a throne would.

The first palaces were built around 1900 BC and destroyed around 1700 BC, probably by earthquakes. They were rebuilt on an even grander scale. This second palace period was Minoan Crete at its height, and it ended with destructions across the island around 1450 BC. After that, only Knossos still worked as a palace, now run in Greek with Linear B, as you will see in The Mycenaeans.

blocks.title: Reading the evidence
blocks.q: A room in a palace holds thirty tall jars and a few clay labels marked with signs. What was the room most likely for?
steps: Many large jars mean storage of liquids or grain.
Labels with writing mean someone was keeping track of the contents.
So it was a storeroom managed by palace officials.
blocks.a: A storeroom, with records of what it held.

blocks.title: Which is a Cretan palace?
blocks.q: Which of these is a palace site on Crete: Pylos, Malia, Thebes?
steps: Pylos is on the west coast of the mainland and Thebes is in central Greece; both are Mycenaean palaces.
Malia is on the north coast of Crete, east of Knossos.

blocks.html: While the palaces of Knossos and the Cretan Palaces flourished on Crete, a different culture grew on the mainland. We call its people the Mycenaeans, after Mycenae, the hilltop citadel in the Peloponnese where rich royal graves were found in the 1870s. They spoke Greek, the language that would later give us Homer, Plato and the New Testament.

The Mycenaeans were Greek speakers of the mainland in the Late Bronze Age, from about 1600 BC. They built palace states at Mycenae, Pylos, Thebes, Tiryns and elsewhere, and by about 1450 BC Greek speakers also ran Knossos on Crete. Their records are in Linear B.

blocks.html: The Mycenaeans learned a great deal from Crete: styles of painting, crafts and, above all, writing. They took the Minoan script, Linear A, and adapted it to write Greek. The result was Linear B. After the destructions on Crete around 1450 BC, Knossos itself was run by Greek speakers, and its huge archive of tablets is in Linear B. How that came about, by conquest or by some other road, is still debated.

Why are we sure the Mycenaeans spoke Greek? Because their tablets, read with the values Michael Ventris worked out in 1952, give Greek words: ti-ri-po (tripod), ka-ko (bronze), wa-na-ka (king). The same values turn thousands of words into Greek, which chance cannot do. You will follow that story in The Breakthrough: Cretan Place Names.

Treating Minoans and Mycenaeans as one people, or treating the Mycenaeans as Homer's heroes exactly as the poems tell them. They were two cultures with different languages. And Homer's Iliad and Odyssey were composed centuries after the palaces fell; they remember some old things, like boar's-tusk helmets, but they are poems, not records. Check yourself: ask whether a "fact" comes from a tablet or a dig, or from a poem written much later.

Each Mycenaean palace ruled its own region. Pylos ran the southwest Peloponnese; Thebes ruled part of Boeotia; Mycenae and Tiryns stood close together in the Argolid. Their tablets name a ruler, the wa-na-ka, and officials below him (see The Wanax and the Lawagetas). The palaces kept careful accounts of flocks, land, workers, bronze and offerings until their fall around 1200 BC.

Linear B writes Greek.

steps: Linear B writes Greek, the Mycenaeans' language.
After the destructions around 1450 BC, Knossos was run by Greek speakers.
Their officials kept the records in their own language, using the script adapted from Linear A.
blocks.a: Because Greek speakers ran Knossos in its later phase.

blocks.html: In The Minoans of Crete and The Mycenaeans you met dates like "about 1450 BC". Where do such numbers come from? No Minoan or Mycenaean text gives a year. Archaeologists build the dates in three steps, and each step has some give in it.

Aegean dates come from pottery sequences (which layer is older), tied to years by radiocarbon and by links to Egypt's dated history. They are approximate, often by decades, and some, like the eruption of Thera, are debated.

Pottery breaks easily, is thrown away constantly and changes style over time, so every dig is full of it. Evans divided Crete's Bronze Age into Early, Middle and Late Minoan by pottery style, each split further (Late Minoan IA, IB, II, and so on). On the mainland the same scheme is called Helladic (Late Helladic is the Mycenaean age), and in the islands, Cycladic. These names tell you which came first, not how many years ago.

blocks.text: Steps 2 and 3: tying the order to years

items: Links to Egypt. Minoan pots turn up in Egyptian tombs, and Egyptian objects on Crete. Egypt's kings can be dated from its own records, so a Minoan style found with a datable Egyptian object gets a date too.
Radiocarbon. Living things take in carbon-14, which decays at a known rate after they die. Measuring what is left in seeds, wood or bone gives a date, with a margin of error.

blocks.html: Why do the methods sometimes disagree? Each has its own uncertainty: a pot can stay in use for decades before it is buried, Egyptian dates themselves have some give, and radiocarbon dates come with error ranges and need careful calibration. When two methods point to different centuries, scholars debate which to trust.

The eruption of Thera (Santorini) buried the town of Akrotiri. Radiocarbon dating points to about 1600 BC; the older dating from links with Egypt pointed to about 1500 BC. The question is still debated, so this course says "about 1600 BC, perhaps later".

Reading "c. 1450 BC" as an exact year. "c." stands for circa, "about", and Aegean dates can be off by decades or more. Check yourself: a question on this site will ask for an order or a period, never for an exact Bronze Age year, and you should treat any exact year you see elsewhere with care.

steps: The Minoan periods run Early, Middle, Late.
Middle comes before Late.

blocks.q: A book dates the end of the second Cretan palaces to "c. 1450 BC". Could the real date be 1470 BC?

Aegean dates come from pottery, radiocarbon and links to Egypt, each with a margin.
A date 20 years off is well within that margin.

blocks.html: The Mycenaean palaces of The Mycenaeans kept their accounts for about two centuries. Then, around 1200 BC, they fell one after another. Pylos burned. Mycenae, Tiryns and Thebes suffered destructions. Within a generation or two the palace system was gone, and with it the need for scribes. Linear B went out of use, and Greece had no writing at all for about four hundred years.

blocks.name: sc-timeline
blocks.cap: From the Linear B palaces to the Greek alphabet. Notice the gap after the palaces fall.

blocks.html: Around 1200 BC the mainland palaces were destroyed, Pylos by fire, and writing disappeared from Greece for about four centuries. Scholars debate the causes; most think several worked together.

The destructions did not all come in one year; they came in waves over decades around 1200 BC. The wider eastern Mediterranean was in trouble at the same time: the Hittite empire in Anatolia collapsed, and cities on the coast of the Levant were destroyed. Many explanations have been offered, and none fits every site.

blocks.html: Many scholars now speak of a systems collapse: palace states that depended on long trade routes and tight central control were fragile, so a few shocks at once could bring the whole network down. That idea is popular, but it is still a debate, not a settled answer.

Why did writing vanish with the palaces? Because Linear B was only ever a tool of palace bookkeeping. A small number of trained scribes wrote it (see Scribes and Their Hands). When there were no palaces to keep accounts for, no one needed scribes, and no one taught the script. Ordinary people had never used it for letters or stories, so it did not survive.

The fire was a disaster for the people of Pylos and a gift to us. The tablets were unbaked clay, and the burning palace baked about a thousand of them hard. You will see why in Clay, Fire and Survival.

Looking for one single cause, such as "the Dorians invaded" or "an earthquake did it". The evidence points in several directions, and most scholars think more than one factor played a part. Check yourself: an answer that names one cause as certain is overclaiming.

blocks.title: What came next?
blocks.q: After the palaces fell around 1200 BC, when did the Greeks write again, and with what?
steps: Linear B disappears with the palaces.
Greek writing returns around 800 BC with letters borrowed from the Phoenician script.
That is a gap of about four centuries.
blocks.a: Around 800 BC, with the Greek alphabet.

blocks.title: Weighing a statement
blocks.q: "The Mycenaean palaces were destroyed by the Sea Peoples in 1200 BC." Is this established?
steps: The Sea Peoples are one proposed cause among several.
The destructions came in waves over decades, not in one year.
So the statement turns one debated idea into a fact.
blocks.a: No; it is one debated explanation, stated too firmly.

blocks.html: What came after the palaces, and how Greek was written again, is the story of Then Came the Alphabet.

You already read and write one kind of script: an alphabet, where each letter stands for one sound (more or less). But that is only one way to write. Every writing system ever invented uses one or more of three kinds of sign, and knowing which is which is the first skill a decipherer needs.

A logogram stands for a whole word or thing. A syllabogram stands for a syllable, such as ka or po. A letter of an alphabet stands for a single sound. Linear B is mostly syllable signs, with logograms for the things it counts.

blocks.html: Why does the number of signs matter so much? A language has only a few dozen sounds, a few dozen to a hundred or so syllables, but thousands of words. So an alphabet needs about two dozen signs, a syllabary several dozen and a word-sign script many hundreds. When scholars counted the Linear B signs (about 87 syllable signs, plus many logograms used with numbers), they knew it had to be mostly a syllabary, before they could read a word.

Most ancient scripts mix kinds. Egyptian hieroglyphs use sound signs and word signs together. Linear B spells words with syllable signs and uses logograms beside numbers to say what is counted: a man, a woman, a horse, a tripod, wheat, oil. Even English mixes them: the digits 0 to 9, & and @ are logograms.

blocks.cap: A short Linear B line: the word i-qo (horse) in two syllable signs, then the horse logogram and the number 2. Tap a sign.

blocks.html: Thinking every ancient script is picture-writing. A few signs look like what they mean (the Linear B horse sign looks like a horse's head), but in a word like i-qo the signs stand for sounds, not pictures. Check: if a sign appears inside many unrelated words, it is a sound sign; if it stands alone before a number, it is probably a logogram.

blocks.title: Count the signs
blocks.q: A script has about 25 different signs, used over and over. What kind of script is it most likely?
steps: About 25 signs is far too few for word signs or for most syllabaries.
It is about the number of sounds in a language.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: In the line 𐀂𐀦 𐂃 𐄈, what kind of sign is the third sign, the horse's head?
steps: The first two signs, i and qo, spell the word i-qo, "horse".
The horse's head stands alone before the number: it says what is counted.

blocks.html: Next, How a Syllabary Works shows how a syllabary is built.

In Word Signs, Syllables and Letters you met the syllabogram, a sign for a whole syllable. Linear B is a syllabary: almost every one of its sound signs stands for either a vowel alone or a consonant followed by a vowel.

A syllabary gives each syllable its own sign: a, e, i, o, u for the vowels alone, then ka, ke, ki, ko, ku, and so on. Laid out with consonants down the side and vowels across the top, the signs fill a grid.

blocks.cap: Part of the Linear B grid. Each row shares a consonant; each column shares a vowel. Tap a sign to see its value and words that use it.

blocks.html: Why is the grid such a good way to think about a syllabary? Because it turns a list of 60 or so signs into a pattern: 13 rows times 5 columns. If you learn that two signs share a row, you know they share a consonant, even before you know what that consonant is. That idea was the key to the decipherment (see Building the Grid).

Treating a syllable sign as a letter. 𐀏 is one sign for two sounds, k and a. There is no separate Linear B sign for k by itself. So you cannot "take the k" out of ka; if a Greek word has a k with no vowel after it, the scribe must choose another way to write it (see Every Sign Ends in a Vowel). Check: count the syllables in a word; that is how many signs it uses.
A few cells are empty: Linear B has no sign for ji, wu or qu, for example. And besides the grid there are some extra signs for special syllables, which you will meet in Special Signs.

blocks.html: Linear B was not the first script of the Aegean. It had two older relatives on Crete. The oldest is called Cretan hieroglyphs, used from about 2100 or 1900 BC to about 1700 BC, in the age of the first palaces you met in Knossos and the Cretan Palaces.

Cretan hieroglyphs are Crete's earliest script, found mostly on seals and on some clay documents, from about 2100 or 1900 BC to about 1700 BC. For most of its life it was used alongside Linear A. It is still unread.

Most of the inscriptions are short, carved on seal stones that were pressed into clay to mark ownership or approval. There are also clay bars, labels and sealings, many from Malia and Knossos. The signs are more picture-like than those of Linear A: heads, hands, animals, tools. Like Linear B, the script seems to mix syllable signs with word signs and has its own numerals. Only a few hundred inscriptions survive, nearly all very short.

blocks.html: Why did Crete use two scripts at once? No one knows for sure. Cretan hieroglyphs appear in the north and east of the island, Linear A first in the south, around Phaistos. They may have been used by different palaces or offices, or for different jobs. Many signs and even some words appear in both, which suggests they belong to the same tradition of Cretan writing.

Confusing Cretan hieroglyphs with Egyptian hieroglyphs. They share only the nickname "hieroglyphs", given because both look picture-like. They are separate scripts with different signs, and the Cretan script writes an unknown language, while Egyptian has been read since the 1820s. Check: if a text is on a Cretan seal, it is not Egyptian.

The famous Phaistos Disc, a clay disc stamped with signs in a spiral, is often lumped in with Cretan hieroglyphs. It is a single object, its signs are not those of the usual script, and its relation to the other Cretan scripts is uncertain. This course leaves it aside.

blocks.title: Older or younger?
blocks.q: Which began first: Cretan hieroglyphs or Linear B?
steps: Cretan hieroglyphs began around 2100 or 1900 BC.
Linear B appears around 1450 BC.

blocks.title: Read or unread?
blocks.q: Can scholars read Cretan hieroglyphs today?
steps: The language behind them is unknown, the texts are few and short, and there is no bilingual text.
Like Linear A, the script remains undeciphered.

blocks.html: In A Family of Aegean Scripts you will see how these Cretan scripts connect to Linear B and to the scripts of Cyprus.

You have now met three Cretan scripts (Cretan Hieroglyphs, Linear A and Linear B). They belong to a family, and the family reaches as far as Cyprus. Knowing who borrowed from whom explains why Linear B can be read and why its relatives help with Linear A.

Linear A gave rise to Linear B, which the Mycenaeans adapted to write Greek. On Cyprus, Cypro-Minoan (probably adapted from Linear A) gave rise to the Cypriot syllabary, which also wrote Greek and was read in the 1870s.

blocks.html: Linear A and Linear B share many sign shapes; you can see that in Signs Shared with Linear B. The Mycenaeans kept the signs, dropped some, added some, and used them for Greek. On Cyprus the line ran separately: Cypro-Minoan, then the Cypriot syllabary, used for Greek well into Classical times. That syllabary was read in the 1870s, with the help of an inscription from Idalion written in both Phoenician and Cypriot Greek.

Why does the family matter? Because related scripts often keep sound values with their shapes. Some Cypriot signs look like Linear B signs and have similar values, which gave scholars a check on their readings. And when scholars read Linear A, they borrow the Linear B values for the shared signs, on the assumption that the values carried over with the shapes. That is a useful working guess, not proof.

Thinking Linear B is the oldest Aegean script, or that it grew out of the Greek alphabet. It is the youngest of the Cretan scripts, adapted from Linear A, and it died out around 1200 BC, about four centuries before the alphabet arrived. Check: put the scripts on the timeline; Linear B sits between Linear A and the alphabet, with a long gap after it.

blocks.html: When the palaces fell around 1200 BC (The End of the Palaces), Linear B fell with them. For about four centuries no one in Greece wrote anything we have found. When the Greeks wrote again, it was with a completely different system: an alphabet borrowed from the Phoenicians, the traders of the Levant coast.
Around 800 BC the Greeks adapted the Phoenician letters to write Greek, adding letters for vowels. The Greek alphabet did not come from Linear B; by then Linear B had been forgotten.

blocks.html: The Phoenician script had about 22 letters, all for consonants; readers supplied the vowels. Greek has many words that begin or end with vowels, and some Phoenician letters stood for sounds Greek did not use. The Greeks reused those letters for vowels: Phoenician ʾalep became alpha (A), he became epsilon (E), and so on. The result was an alphabet with letters for vowels as well as consonants, the ancestor of the Latin letters you are reading now.

blocks.html: Why could the alphabet write Greek so much better? Because each letter is one sound, so clusters like khr- or final -s are easy: χρυσός. A syllabary of open syllables cannot write a consonant without a vowel, so Linear B had to bend Greek to fit, as you will see in Every Sign Ends in a Vowel. With an alphabet, writing spread beyond a few palace scribes to many people, and the first Greek poems written down, such as Homer's, followed.

Assuming the Greek alphabet grew out of Linear B. The shapes, the kind of script and the dates all say no: the alphabet came from Phoenician, and it appeared long after the last Linear B scribe had died. Check: alpha (Α) comes from the Phoenician letter ʾalep, not from the Linear B sign 𐀀.

blocks.title: How long was the gap?
blocks.q: Linear B ended around 1200 BC and the alphabet appears around 800 BC. About how many years passed with no writing in Greece?
steps: Both dates are BC, so subtract: 1200 − 800.
That is 400 years.

blocks.title: Spot the source
blocks.q: Which script is the Greek alphabet's parent: Linear B, Phoenician or Egyptian hieroglyphs?
steps: The Greek letter names (alpha, beta, gamma) echo the Phoenician names (ʾalep, bet, gimel).
The shapes match Phoenician letters, and the date fits.

blocks.html: In the 1890s a British archaeologist named Arthur Evans went to Crete looking for something small: seal stones engraved with signs, which some Cretans still wore as charms. Evans suspected the signs were writing, older than anything then known in Europe. He bought land at Knossos, near modern Heraklion, the site of the palace you met in Knossos and the Cretan Palaces.

Evans began digging at Knossos in March 1900. Within weeks he found clay tablets covered in signs, and over the following years thousands more. He named the civilization "Minoan", sorted the scripts into Cretan hieroglyphs, Linear A and Linear B, and was convinced their language was not Greek.

The tablets turned up in room after room. Most were in the script Evans called Linear B ("linear" because the signs are drawn with lines rather than pictures; "B" because it was a later, more regular form than Linear A). Linear A tablets came from other Cretan sites, especially Hagia Triada. In 1909 Evans published the first volume of Scripta Minoa, on the Cretan scripts.

blocks.text: What Evans could and could not see

blocks.html: Evans worked out a good deal. He saw that the tablets were accounts. He recognized the numerals, and he saw that some signs were pictures of what was counted: men, horses, chariots, vessels. He even noticed that some words changed their endings. But he could not read them, and he made two choices that slowed everyone down.

items: He kept most of the tablets unpublished. Evans wanted to publish them himself and did not finish. Most Knossos Linear B texts appeared only in 1952, after his death in 1941. Scholars outside his circle had little to work with for decades.
He was sure the language was Minoan, not Greek. He saw the mainland Mycenaeans as a colonial offshoot of Crete, so Greek seemed impossible to him and to most who followed him.

blocks.html: Why did Evans's view carry so much weight? He had found the tablets, he owned the site and he was the most famous archaeologist of the Aegean. When the leading authority says the language cannot be Greek, few test the idea. Ventris himself, who heard Evans lecture in 1936, long expected the answer to be some other language.

Assuming the excavator understood what he found. Evans discovered the tablets, named the scripts and made important observations, but his firm belief that the tablets were not Greek held back the idea that Linear B could be Greek. Check yourself: separate what Evans found (tablets, signs, numerals) from what he believed (their language), and treat the second as a hypothesis.

blocks.html: The story continues on the mainland with Carl Blegen at Pylos. For the full story told as one long read, see How Linear B Was Deciphered.

For almost forty years after Arthur Evans at Knossos, 1900, Linear B looked like a Cretan script. Then, in 1939, the American archaeologist Carl Blegen began digging on a hill near Pylos, in the southwest Peloponnese, where he hoped to find the palace of Nestor, the old king of Pylos in Homer.

On the first day of the 1939 dig, Blegen's team found the palace's archive room, full of Linear B tablets. The Second World War stopped the work; it resumed in 1952, and many more tablets came out. Pylos proved Linear B was the script of the mainland palaces too.

blocks.html: If Linear B had been found only at Knossos, Evans's idea of a purely Minoan script could survive. A large archive at Pylos, in the middle of the Greek mainland, changed the picture. The mainland palaces, centuries later home to Greek speakers, used the same script. That made Greek a reasonable guess for its language, though most scholars still did not take it seriously.

blocks.html: The Pylos tablets also gave scholars something they badly needed: a large set of texts published quickly and carefully. Bennett's edition of 1951 put good copies of the Pylos texts into scholars' hands, which Evans's Knossos tablets had never been. Ventris used it in the months before his breakthrough.

Why does more text help a decipherer so much? Every pattern you find, such as an ending that changes or a word that repeats, must be seen many times before it can be trusted. A few hundred short tablets cannot show that; thousands can. Pylos and Knossos together gave Linear B enough text for the patterns to show. Linear A, as you will see in Why Linear A Can't Be Read Yet, has far less.

Thinking Linear B was found only on Crete. It was found first at Knossos, but Pylos, Mycenae, Thebes, Tiryns and other mainland sites have Linear B too. Check: Linear B on the map spreads across the mainland; Linear A stays mostly on Crete and the islands.

Ventris announced his result in 1952.

blocks.title: What changed?
blocks.q: Before 1939, what was the strongest argument that Linear B was only a Cretan script?
steps: All known Linear B tablets came from Knossos, on Crete.
Pylos showed it was also used on the mainland.
blocks.a: All the tablets came from Knossos, until Pylos.

blocks.html: The tablets that Evans and Blegen found (Carl Blegen at Pylos) have lasted more than three thousand years. You might think they were made to last. They were not. They survived by accident, and the accident was fire.

Linear B tablets were made of damp clay, dried in the sun and meant for one season's records; the clay could be softened and reused. When the palaces burned, the fires baked the tablets hard and preserved them.

A scribe pressed a lump of damp clay into a flat page or a long, narrow leaf and drew the signs with a pointed stylus. The tablet dried in the air. It was a working note: a count of sheep, a delivery of oil, a list of workers. Most records seem to cover only the current year; older ones were thrown away or the clay was reused. Important totals may have been copied onto something else, perhaps a material that has not survived.

blocks.name: sc-tablet
blocks.cap: A single-entry leaf in the style of the Knossos sheep tablets. A tablet like this was a quick note, not a document meant for the ages.

blocks.html: Why did fire save the tablets? Unbaked clay is soft; in water it slowly turns back into mud. Heat changes clay chemically into a hard, stable material, like a pot from a kiln. When Pylos burned around 1200 BC, the archive room was baked, and so were about a thousand tablets. At Knossos, fire did the same. We have the tablets because the buildings were destroyed.

Thinking the tablets were fired on purpose to last. Scribes did not bake them; they were meant to be temporary. Check: a tablet's date is the date of the fire that baked it, so each archive is a snapshot of the palace's last months, not a long history.

This has a big consequence for what we can learn. Each archive shows a short slice of time, roughly the last year of the palace. At Pylos we see the palace's business in its final season: flocks, rations, bronze for smiths and offerings to the gods. We do not see how things changed over generations.

Only those caught in a fire were baked hard; the rest returned to mud or were reused.

blocks.html: Before you can study a script, you need a way to talk about its signs. In Arthur Evans at Knossos, 1900 you saw that Evans kept most of the tablets to himself. When the Pylos tablets were published in 1951, the American scholar Emmett L. Bennett Jr. sorted every Linear B sign into a numbered list. Scholars still use his numbers.

Each Linear B sign has a number in a standard list, written with an asterisk: *08 is the sign read a, *01 is da, *70 is ko. A sign whose value is still unknown is written by its number alone, like *18.

blocks.cap: A few signs with their numbers. The numbers are labels in a list; the values came later.

blocks.html: Sorting signs is harder than it sounds. Two scribes may draw the same sign quite differently, and two different signs may look alike. Bennett compared thousands of examples to decide which shapes were variants of one sign and which were separate signs. Then he gave each a number. Now two scholars on different continents could write "*70" and mean exactly the same sign, with no guessing about its sound.

blocks.name: sc-signs
blocks.cap: ko-no-so (Knossos) with each sign numbered and its Bennett number in the breakdown. Tap a sign.

blocks.html: Why did a neutral number matter so much? Because any name that hints at a sound biases the reader. If you call a sign "the ka sign" before you know its value, you start seeing ka everywhere. A number is a label with no meaning, so it lets you count, compare and sort signs fairly. Alice Kober and Michael Ventris both worked with signs as numbered shapes before any sound was known.

Treating a sign number as a sound. *08 does not mean "eight" or any sound; it is only the sign's place in the list. Its value, a, was found later, by the decipherment. Check: you can say "*08 is a", but never "*08 sounds like 8".

The numbering was adopted by scholars as the standard in the 1960s and is still used, with additions. When you read a transliteration such as *18-to, the asterisk number tells you the scribe wrote a sign whose value is not agreed (Signs Still Unread). Logograms have numbers too: the man sign is *100, the horse *105, the tripod *201.

a-mi-ni-so begins with that sign.

blocks.q: A word has a sign whose value nobody knows, Bennett number 47, followed by da. How do scholars write it?
steps: An unread sign is written by its number with an asterisk.

blocks.html: With the signs numbered (Numbering the Signs) and a grid in mind (How a Syllabary Works), you are ready for the first great step. It was taken in New York in the 1940s by Alice Kober, a classics professor at Brooklyn College, working in her spare time on a script nobody could read.

Kober showed, without guessing a single sound, that Linear B words change their endings. In sets of three related forms she found signs that must share a consonant, and others that must share a vowel. Her method was to avoid guessing.

Kober (1906 to 1950) refused to guess what language the tablets were in. Others had tried to "read" Linear B as Etruscan, Hittite and other languages, and every guess had failed. She studied the signs as shapes instead, keeping thousands of hand-written index cards: which signs came together, which began or ended words, how often each appeared. In papers from 1945 to 1948 she showed that the language had endings that changed with grammar, as Latin and Greek do.

Kober noticed sets of words that shared a beginning and differed at the end, in three forms. Here is a set of that kind, written with the values we know today (Kober had no values; she saw only the shapes):

blocks.cap: Knossos, Knossian (masculine), Knossian (feminine). The third sign changes from form 1 to forms 2 and 3.

blocks.html: Look at the shapes only. Forms 2 and 3 share three signs and then differ in the last one. Form 1 has the same first two signs but a different third sign. Kober reasoned: the stem ends in a consonant. In form 1 that consonant is written together with one vowel; in forms 2 and 3 with another. So the third sign of form 1 and the third sign of forms 2 and 3 share a consonant (today we know: so and si, both s). And the last signs of forms 2 and 3 share their own consonant (jo and ja, both j) while differing in vowel.

blocks.html: Why do the "bridging" signs prove a shared consonant? In a syllabary every sign ends in a vowel. If a stem ends in a consonant, that consonant cannot stand alone; it must be written with whatever vowel follows it. When the ending changes, the vowel changes, so the scribe has to switch to a different sign with the same consonant. The switch exposes a pair of signs in the same row of the grid.

Thinking Kober guessed at sounds or a language. She did the opposite: she proved relationships between signs from patterns alone. Check: her results say "these two signs share a consonant", never "this sign is s". The sounds came after her death, from Ventris.

In 1948 Kober drew a small grid of ten signs showing which shared a consonant and which shared a vowel. She died in May 1950, at 43, two years before the decipherment. John Chadwick later judged her work the most valuable before Ventris's.

blocks.title: Find the bridge
blocks.q: Three forms share a stem: Word 1 ends in sign X; Words 2 and 3 have sign Y where Word 1 has X, then one more sign. Which two signs share a consonant?
steps: The stem ends in a consonant, written with a different vowel in Word 1 than in Words 2 and 3.
So the sign at that spot in Word 1 (X) and in Words 2 and 3 (Y) must share that consonant.

blocks.title: With values
blocks.q: In ko-no-so and ko-no-si-jo, which signs share a consonant because of the changing ending?
steps: The third signs differ: so in one, si in the other.
Both begin with s, the end of the stem Knos-.

blocks.html: Alice Kober's pairs (Alice Kober's Triplets) said which signs shared a consonant or a vowel. Michael Ventris, a young British architect who had been fascinated by the tablets since he heard Arthur Evans lecture in 1936, at the age of 14, took the next step. He put the relations into one big table: the grid.

Ventris arranged signs in a grid so that all signs in one row shared a consonant and all signs in one column shared a vowel, before he knew what any of those consonants and vowels were. Sounds came last: once a few cells were known, the grid passed them along whole rows and columns.

blocks.name: sc-grid
blocks.cap: Build a grid the way Kober and Ventris did. Place each sign by the clues so that rows share a consonant and columns share a vowel; then add the sounds.

blocks.html: Ventris worked through 1951 and 1952, sending his results to other scholars in a series of work notes. His grids had numbered rows and columns but no sounds. He filled them with evidence like Kober's: endings that changed, spelling variants of one word, signs that appeared at the start of words (probably plain vowels, since a syllabary needs vowel signs to begin words like a-mi-ni-so). Every placement was a claim he could test against the next tablet.

vowel 2
vowel 3

blocks.html: Why is a grid so powerful? It multiplies every discovery. If you learn that one sign in a row begins with s, every sign in that row begins with s. If you learn that one sign in a column ends in o, every sign in that column ends in o. So one secure value can fix five signs, and two crossing values can fix a whole corner. That is how a handful of good guesses could unlock the script.

Assuming the grid was filled with sounds from the start. It began as relationships only: "these signs share something". Ventris changed his grid many times as evidence came in. Check: in a grid built this way, a cell can be correctly placed long before anyone knows its value.
The full Linear B grid today has 13 rows (the vowels alone and 12 consonants) and 5 columns. Explore it in the sign grid.

blocks.q: Sign X is in the same row as ko and the same column as ti. What is its value?
steps: Same row as ko: X begins with k.
Same column as ti: X ends in i.
Put them together: k + i.

blocks.title: Pass a value along
blocks.q: A row holds four signs whose values are unknown. You learn that one of them is na. What do you now know about the other three?
steps: Signs in one row share a consonant.
na begins with n.
blocks.a: They all begin with n (ne, ni, no or nu).

blocks.html: By the spring of 1952 Ventris had a grid (Building the Grid) with rows and columns but very few sounds. He needed a way in: a few words whose sounds he could guess with confidence. He found them in a pattern he had noticed. Some words appeared only on the Knossos tablets, never at Pylos.

Ventris guessed that words found only at Knossos were Cretan place names, and he tried names known from later Greek: ko-no-so (Knossos), a-mi-ni-so (Amnisos) and tu-ri-so (Tylissos). The values fit his grid, and when he put them into other words, those words began to look like Greek.

blocks.html: Place names are a decipherer's best friend. They often survive changes of language and rule, so a name used in the Bronze Age may still be known centuries later. Knossos, Amnisos and Tylissos are all named by later Greek writers. And a word that appears only in the records of one region is likely to name something in that region.

blocks.html: The test came next. Ventris put the new values through his grid, so each guessed value fixed others in its row and column. Then he read other words. Some came out as Greek: ko-wo and ko-wa (boy and girl), ka-ko (bronze), po-ro (foal, beside young horses). He had expected a language like Etruscan, and at first he doubted his own result.

Why is this a proof and not a lucky match? A single name could fit by chance. But the values from three names, passed through the grid, gave readings for dozens of other signs, and those readings turned many unrelated words into recognizable Greek, with Greek endings in the right grammatical places. Chance cannot do that across thousands of words.

Thinking one lucky word proved the decipherment. A few names gave values; the proof was that those values then turned many other words into Greek, and kept doing so on new tablets (see The Tripod Tablet Confirms It). Check: ask of any claimed decipherment, "what happens to all the other words?"

blocks.title: Values from a name
blocks.q: If 𐀒𐀜𐀰 is Knossos, what values must its three signs have?
steps: Knossos, written in open syllables, is ko-no-so: the k and n are split by an empty vowel, the double s is written once, the final s is dropped.
So the signs are ko, no and so.

blocks.title: Pass it on
blocks.q: If the third sign of ko-no-so is so, what do you know about every other sign in its row?
steps: Signs in one row share a consonant.
blocks.a: They all begin with s: sa, se, si, su.

blocks.html: In The Breakthrough: Cretan Place Names you saw the breakthrough. Now the story moves fast. On 1 July 1952 Michael Ventris, then 29 years old, gave a talk on BBC radio. He told listeners that the tablets of Knossos and Pylos were written in Greek, "a difficult and archaic Greek", as he put it, but Greek.

Ventris announced on BBC radio on 1 July 1952 that Linear B was Greek. John Chadwick, a Cambridge scholar of early Greek, heard the talk and joined him; in 1953 they published the case in the Journal of Hellenic Studies.

blocks.name: sc-timeline
blocks.cap: The discovery and decipherment, AD 1900 to 1956. Tap an event to read more.

blocks.html: Ventris had not set out to prove Linear B was Greek. In 1940, still a teenager, he published an article arguing that the language was related to Etruscan, and he kept looking in that direction into the early 1950s. When Greek words began to appear, he treated the idea with suspicion at first, half expecting it to collapse. It did not.

John Chadwick, a lecturer at Cambridge who had worked on codebreaking during the war, heard the broadcast and wrote to Ventris. Chadwick knew early Greek dialects deeply; Ventris knew the script. Together they wrote "Evidence for Greek Dialect in the Mycenaean Archives", published in 1953. In 1956 came their book Documents in Mycenaean Greek. That September, weeks before the book appeared, Ventris was killed in a road accident, aged 34.

blocks.html: Why did Ventris's surprise make his case stronger? A person who wants a certain answer can find it almost anywhere, by bending the evidence. Ventris wanted Etruscan, so Greek was the answer the evidence forced on him, not one he forced on the evidence. Good decipherments often look like this: the data push the decipherer somewhere unexpected.

Imagining Ventris set out to prove Linear B was Greek. He expected something like Etruscan, and the Greek results surprised him. Check: his 1940 article argued for a link with Etruscan; Greek came from the grid, not from his hopes.

blocks.html: An announcement is not a proof. After Greek, 1952, the decisive test was a new text: one that Ventris had never seen, read with his values exactly as they stood. If the values were right, it would make sense. If they were wrong, it would be nonsense. That text came out of the ground at Pylos.

On Pylos tablet Ta 641, cleaned and read in 1953, the words read with Ventris's values describe the pictured vessels: ti-ri-po beside a tripod, and cups described as having four, three or no handles beside cups with four, three or no handles.

blocks.html: Blegen's team found the tablet in June 1952, the season after the war. It was cleaned enough to read in the spring of 1953. On 16 May 1953 Blegen wrote to Ventris that the words matched the pictures, adding "All this seems too good to be true. Is coincidence excluded?" Here is why he was so struck.

blocks.html: Notice qe-to-ro-we. It begins with qe, the q row, which Ventris had read as a kʷ sound. "Four" in early Greek began with kʷ, like Latin quattuor. The handles on the picture confirm the q value, a value no one could have chosen to fit this tablet in advance.

Why is this such strong evidence? The tablet carries two independent kinds of information: pictures, which anyone can see, and words, which need the sound values. Ventris fixed his values before the tablet was read. If the values were wrong, the words beside the four-handled cup would be gibberish. Instead they said "four-handled". The pictures acted as a built-in answer key.

Thinking everyone agreed at once. Most specialists were convinced within a few years, but some, such as the scholar Arthur Beattie, argued against the decipherment for a long time. The tripod tablet did much to persuade the doubters. Check: a decipherment wins acceptance by passing tests over years, not by one announcement.

blocks.title: Read the handles
blocks.q: On Ta 641, ti-ri-jo-we stands beside a cup sign. How many handles should that cup have?
steps: ti-ri- is "three", as in tripod.
-o-we is "eared", that is, "handled".

blocks.title: Two tripods
blocks.q: The word ti-ri-po-de stands before the tripod sign. What number would you expect after the sign?

Five signs stand for a vowel by itself: a, e, i, o and u. They are the first row of the grid, and they write a vowel that has no consonant before it, at the start of a word (a-mi-ni-so) or after another vowel (pa-i-to).

blocks.html: Why does a syllabary need separate vowel signs at all? Because the other signs always begin with a consonant. A word like Amnisos starts with the sound a, with nothing before it. Without a sign for a alone, the scribe could not begin the word. In the grid, the vowel row is the row whose "consonant" is nothing.

Mixing up signs that look alike. 𐀀 (a) and 𐁀 (a2, read ha) both look like a branching stem; 𐀂 (i) and 𐀩 (re) both have upward prongs. Learn each vowel with its own shape and check the details: a's arms bend down, i has three prongs and a crossbar. The flashcards have a vowel deck for practice.

blocks.html: Why learn sign by sign instead of by row? Because the shapes do not follow the grid. The grid groups signs by sound, but the signs were inherited from Linear A, where their shapes had their own history. 𐀏 (a circle with a cross) and 𐀐 share nothing in their drawing. So the grid tells you what a sign means once you know it; it cannot tell you how to recognize it.

Expecting signs in one row to look alike. 𐀏 𐀐 𐀑 𐀒 𐀓 all begin with k, yet they look nothing like each other. Check: learn each sign with an anchor word: ka from ka-ko, ko from ko-no-so, pa from pa-te, ma from ma-te, di from di-pa.

j and w are glides (y and w sounds); q writes the old Greek labiovelars kʷ, gʷ and kʷʰ, which later became p, b, t or d; r writes both r and l; z writes a sound like dz. The j, q, w and z rows have empty cells.

items: r writes r and l. Greek had both sounds, but Linear B had one set of signs for them. So pa-ra-jo is palaios, old, and me-ri is meli, honey.

q writes a k or g sound made with rounded lips, kʷ or gʷ (and kʷʰ). Early Greek had these sounds; later Greek turned them into p, b, t or d. So qa-si-re-u is later basileus, and qe-to-ro-we begins with the kʷ of "four", like Latin quattuor.

blocks.html: The j row is a y sound, as in "yes", and the w row a w sound. Both are often glides between vowels (Diphthongs and Glides). Greek later lost w altogether, which is why wo-no (woinos, wine) became oinos.

Why are there gaps? A script keeps the signs its writers need. Syllables like ji, wu and qu were rare or impossible in Mycenaean Greek, so no sign for them was needed or kept. That the gaps fall in sensible places is one more sign that the values are right.

Reading q as English "kw" spelled with a q, and thinking it shows a strange, non-Greek sound. In Linear B, q stands for the old Greek labiovelars kʷ, gʷ and kʷʰ, which later became p, b, t or d depending on the vowel and the dialect. Check: qa-si-re-u → basileus (q became b); te-qa → Thebai, Thebes (q became b); qe-to-ro-we has the q of "four" (later τετρα-, with t).

blocks.html: The grid you learned in The d, k, m, n and p Rows and The Other Rows: j, q, r, s, t, w, z covers most Linear B writing. But scribes also had about fourteen extra signs with known values, outside the grid. Scholars call them special signs. They are the reason you see numbers like a2 in transliterations.

Special signs write syllables beyond the plain grid: a2 (ha), a3 (ai), au, pu2 (phu), ra2 (rya), ra3 (rai), ro2 (ryo), ta2 (tya), and clusters like dwe, dwo, nwa, pte, twe and two. They were optional: scribes could usually spell the same word with basic signs.

blocks.html: Why have optional signs at all? Scripts collect useful extras over time. A sign for ha or ai saves a scribe from spelling a sound only roughly, and a cluster sign like two writes in one stroke what would otherwise take two signs. But nothing forced their use, and the same word sometimes appears with and without them. Several of them, such as au, nwa, pu2 and ta2, also appear in Linear A.

Thinking the special signs are required, or that words without them are misspelled. They were optional shortcuts. Check: olive oil appears both as e-ra-wo, with plain ra, and as e-ra3-wo, with the special sign rai; both are correct. The grid is the core of the script; the special signs are extras.

blocks.html: You now know the grid and the special signs (Special Signs). Together they read nearly everything on the tablets. But a small set of signs still has no agreed value. Recall from Numbering the Signs how they are written: by number, with an asterisk.

About fifteen rare signs, such as *18, *47 and *63, have no agreed value. A few have proposed values, such as *56 (perhaps pa3), *79 (perhaps zu) and *82 (perhaps swa), and *65 is read ju only with doubt. The common signs are read with confidence.

blocks.html: A sign is read with confidence when it appears in many words that make sense with its value. Rare signs give little to test. If a sign occurs in only a handful of names, any value would fit, so no value can be proved. Scholars propose values from the contexts and spellings, and some proposals are widely liked, but this course marks them "perhaps".

Why are rare signs harder than common ones? Reading is a test of fit across many cases. The value ko is checked in hundreds of words, from ko-no-so to ko-wo. A sign that appears only in two personal names has nothing to check against; it is like a crossword clue with no crossing words.

Taking the unread signs as proof that Linear B is not really deciphered. They are rare, together only a tiny share of the signs on the tablets. The common signs, which make up nearly all the writing, give good Greek, again and again. Check: count how often unread signs appear in any tablet you read here; usually not at all.

Many of the unread signs turn up mostly in personal names and other words with no later Greek form to compare. New finds can change that: a sign seen in a fresh context, beside a logogram or in a known word, is how proposals for its value get tested.

blocks.html: You can now read the signs. The next skill is reading words, and for that you need to know how a scribe fitted Greek into the script. Everything follows from one fact you met in How a Syllabary Works and The d, k, m, n and p Rows.

Every Linear B sign ends in a vowel. So Linear B can write only open syllables (a consonant plus a vowel, or a vowel alone). Greek words with final consonants or consonant clusters must be bent to fit: some sounds go unwritten, and some consonants get an extra vowel.

Greek is full of consonants that are not followed by a vowel. Look at khalkos, bronze: the l has no vowel after it, and neither does the final s. Look at tripos, tripod: the t and r stand together. A script of open syllables has no sign for l alone, s alone or t alone. The scribes solved this with a few fixed habits, which this unit teaches one at a time:

blocks.html: Why did the scribes accept such rough spelling? The script was inherited from Linear A, built for a different language, perhaps one with mostly open syllables. And it was used by a few trained palace scribes for their own records. A reader who knew the language and the context could fill in the gaps, the way you can read "bldg" or "txt msg". Perfect spelling was never the goal; useful records were.

Expecting the spelling to show every sound. It cannot: a sign always ends in a vowel, so many sounds go unwritten, and some written vowels were never said. Check: never read a Linear B word aloud sign by sign and call that the word. ka-ko was said khalkos, not "kako".

blocks.html: The first way to fit Greek into open syllables (Every Sign Ends in a Vowel) is the simplest: leave some consonants out. The scribes did this in two places, at the end of a word and before another consonant.

Final consonants are not written (l, m, n, r, s), and neither are l, m, n, r and s when they close a syllable before another consonant: ka-ko is khalkos (bronze), pa-ta is panta (all), ko-wo is korwos (boy). A final k sound is written with the vowel before it: wa-na-ka.

items: At the end of a word: l, m, n, r and s are simply left off. Greek words very often end in -s or -n, so this rule is everywhere.
Before another consonant: l, m, n, r and s are left off when they close a syllable. The next consonant starts a new syllable and gets the vowel. So khal-kos loses its l, and pan-ta its n.

blocks.html: One exception: when a word ends in a stop such as the k sound of wanaks, the scribe writes it with the vowel before it, wa-na-ka, and drops the s.

Why these consonants? l, m, n, r and s are "soft" consonants that can trail at the end of a syllable. A syllable-based reader expects each syllable to start with a consonant and end with a vowel; the trailing consonant has no place, so it falls away. Harder stops like t, k and p, when they come first in a cluster, start their own syllable instead; you will meet that in Clusters and Empty Vowels.

Reading the spelled form as the whole word, as if ka-ko were said "kako". The Greek word is khalkos; the spelling leaves out sounds the reader supplied. Check: when a Linear B word looks too short, ask which l, m, n, r or s might be missing before a consonant or at the end.

blocks.html: Dropping consonants (Missing Consonants) handled l, m, n, r and s. But what about clusters that start with a stop, like the tr of tripos or the kn of Knossos? There the scribes did the opposite of dropping: they added a vowel.

Other consonant clusters are split with a vowel borrowed from the next syllable, an "empty" vowel that was written but not said: ko-no-so for Knosos, ti-ri-po for tripos, a-re-ka-sa-da-ra for Aleksandra.

blocks.text: How to find the empty vowel

items: Split the word into sounds: t-r-i-p-o-s.
Find a cluster that is not one of the dropped kinds (l, m, n, r, s before a consonant): here t-r.
Give the first consonant the vowel of the syllable that follows: t + i (from ri) = ti.
Write the rest normally, dropping the final s: ti-ri-po.

blocks.html: Why copy the next vowel rather than any vowel? Because it is the least misleading choice. The empty vowel sits right before a syllable with the same vowel, so a reader who sees ti-ri can tell that the first i echoes the second. It also matches the way the tongue moves straight into the next syllable. The rule is regular enough that scholars can predict spellings with it.

Pronouncing the empty vowel. In ti-ri-po the first i was not said; the word was tripos, two syllables, not three. Check: if a vowel exactly copies the next syllable's vowel and sits between two consonants that could form a Greek cluster (tr, kn, khr, mn, tn, ks, dr), it is probably empty.

One sign, several sounds: r stands for r and l; the p signs cover p, b and ph; the k signs cover k, g and kh; the q signs cover kʷ, gʷ and kʷʰ; the t signs cover t and th. Only d is kept apart from t. And h is usually not written.

blocks.html: Why would a script blur sounds that Greek kept apart? Because it was not designed for Greek. Linear B adapted Linear A's signs, and Linear A's language may not have had all these distinctions. The Mycenaeans added some signs but did not build a full set for b, g, ph, kh and l. Readers coped, because in a list of goods the word was nearly always clear from context.

Thinking pa-ta must contain p and t sounds. pa could be pa, ba or pha; ta could be ta or tha. The reader knew from the word which one was meant. Check: when you turn a spelling back into Greek, try each sound the row allows: p, b or ph; k, g or kh; r or l.

blocks.html: The last spelling habits concern vowels that meet. You saw in One Sign, Several Sounds that h is not written and in Clusters and Empty Vowels how consonant clusters are split. When two vowels stand side by side, or form a diphthong, scribes had a few more habits.

Between vowels a glide often appears: j after i (i-je-re-u, hiereus, priest; po-ti-ni-ja, potnia), and w after u. The u of a diphthong is written (au, eu, ou: ke-ra-me-u, kerameus), but the i of ai, ei and oi is often left out before a consonant (wo-no, woinos).

blocks.html: Say "hiereus" slowly and you will hear a small y sound sliding from the i into the e. The scribes wrote that slide with the j row: i-je. After u they often wrote a w slide instead. These glide signs are not extra consonants of the Greek word; they show how the vowels joined.

A diphthong is two vowels said in one syllable: au, eu, ou, ai, ei, oi. Linear B treated them differently. The u half is written with the vowel sign u (or the special sign au). The i half of ai, ei and oi is often skipped before a consonant, though a scribe could write it (pa-i-to, Phaistos) or use the special signs a3 (ai) and ra3 (rai).

Why learn these habits at all? Because they change how a word looks. Without them, i-je-re-u looks like four syllables of an unknown word, and wo-no looks nothing like oinos. With them you can see the Greek through the spelling: take out the glide, put back the h, the i of the diphthong and the final s. Scholars use exactly these steps to turn spellings into words.

Reading every j or w as a full consonant. Many are glides the scribe wrote between vowels: i-je-re-u is hiereus, not "hi-ye-reus". And the i of a diphthong often disappears: wo-no is woinos. Check: a j right after an i, before another vowel, is almost always a glide.

blocks.html: In Word Signs, Syllables and Letters you met logograms, signs for whole things. Linear B uses more than a hundred of them, and they are the easiest signs on a tablet to spot: they stand alone, right before a number, and many look like what they mean.

A logogram is a sign for a thing (man, woman, horse, tripod, wheat, wine) that stands before a number and says what is being counted. It is not read as part of a sentence; the words around it are spelled in syllable signs.

blocks.html: In transliteration a logogram is written in capital letters, using a short Latin word: VIR for man, MUL for woman (from mulier), EQU for horse (equus), OVIS for sheep, GRA for wheat (granum). Vessels are written by their sign number with VAS ("vessel"): *201VAS is the tripod cauldron. The Latin is only a label scholars agreed on; the scribes never wrote Latin.

Why did the scribes need logograms if they could spell? Speed and clarity. A tablet is a list: the important facts are what and how many. A single sign for "horse" before a number can be read at a glance, by anyone, even without reading the words. And often the word and the logogram appear together: i-qo (horse), then the horse sign, then the number, so one checks the other. That double writing was a gift to Ventris's decipherment.

Confusing logograms with syllable signs, or reading a logogram as a sound. A logogram tells you what is being counted; the words before it are spelled in syllables. Check: a sign that stands alone just before a number is almost always a logogram; signs that run together between dividers are a spelled word.

The next sign stands alone right before the number.
It is the tripod cauldron, *201VAS.

blocks.html: Among the logograms of Logograms are the farm animals: sheep, goats, pigs, cattle and horses. The palaces cared a great deal whether an animal was male or female, because that decided what it was good for: rams for wool, ewes for lambs and milk. So the scribes marked it.

Small marks on an animal logogram show its sex. The ram has two short bars across its stem, the ewe a forked stem; scholars write them OVISm and OVISf. The same marks work for goats, pigs, cattle and horses.

head: Male
Female
blocks.cap: Each animal has one logogram, marked male (m) or female (f).

blocks.name: sc-tablet

blocks.html: Knossos alone has many hundreds of sheep tablets, covering flocks of tens of thousands of animals across Crete. Many flocks are recorded as males, which scholars take to be mostly wethers (castrated males kept for their wool). Those flocks supplied the wool for a large cloth industry recorded on other tablets. By counting OVISm and OVISf across the archive, scholars can see how the palace ran its wool business.

A sheep line usually has several parts: a man's name (the shepherd), a place, then one or more animal signs, each with its own number. A flock might be written OVISm 80 OVISf 20, so you read each logogram with the number right after it: 80 rams and 20 ewes. Add the numbers when a question asks for the whole flock.

blocks.title: Count the flock
blocks.q: A line ends 𐂇 𐄗 𐂆 𐄑. How many sheep in all?
steps: Each logogram has its own number: 80 rams, 20 ewes.

blocks.html: Why add marks instead of drawing different animals? It is economical. One base sign says "sheep"; a small change adds one piece of information. A reader who knows the sheep sign learns all the sheep signs at once. It works the same way for every animal, so the system is easy to learn.

Thinking the two sheep signs are different animals. They are one logogram, sheep, marked male or female. Check: look at the body of the sign first (sheep, goat, pig, cow, horse), then at the small mark for the sex.

steps: pa-i-to is Phaistos, a place.
OVISf is the sheep sign with the female mark.
The number is 50.

blocks.html: Almost every Linear B line ends in a number, so reading numbers is the most useful skill on the tablets. Happily, the Aegean numbers are easy. Linear A uses the same system, so this lesson serves both scripts (Linear A's fractions come in Linear A Numbers and Fractions).

Strokes for ones, bars for tens, circles for hundreds, circles with rays for thousands, and circles with rays and a bar for ten thousands. You add them up, like tally marks. Groups are written largest first, but the order does not change the value.

Mark
Example
rows: a circle with rays and a bar

items: Find each group of marks: rayed circles, circles, bars, strokes.
Count each group.

blocks.html: Why is this "additive" and not "place value" like our digits? In 352 written our way, the 3 means three hundreds only because of where it stands. In Aegean numbers each mark carries its own value wherever it is: a circle is always 100. So you never need a zero: 2,005 is just two rayed circles and five strokes. The cost is that big numbers take many marks.

Treating the numerals as place value, like our digits. Each mark has its own value and you add them, as with Roman numerals but with no subtraction (there is no "IV"-style rule). Check: count circles as hundreds and bars as tens wherever they stand; three bars is 30, not 3.

Totals use the same marks. A Linear B list often ends with a line beginning to-so (tosos, "so many"), followed by the sum of the lines above. Big totals show how large the palace operations were: flocks counted in thousands, grain in hundreds of units.

steps: 2 rayed circles: 2,000.

blocks.html: Counting jars or sheep needs only the numbers of Aegean Numbers. But grain, oil, wine and bronze are not counted; they are measured. Linear B has a system of measures, each with its own sign. Here the arithmetic gets more interesting.

Dry goods: a unit (written with the commodity's own sign), then T (a tenth), V (a sixth of T) and Z (a quarter of V). Liquids: a unit, S (a third), V and Z. Weights: the talent L, then M (a thirtieth), and smaller units below. Each step has its own ratio.

head: System
Steps
So one unit is
rows: 1 unit = 10 T; 1 T = 6 V; 1 V = 4 Z
1 unit = 3 S; 1 S = 6 V; 1 V = 4 Z
1 L = 30 M (and smaller N, P, Q)
blocks.cap: Mycenaean measures. The sizes in liters or kilograms are modern estimates; the ratios are what the tablets show.

blocks.name: sc-numbers
blocks.cap: The dry measures. Switch to liquid and weight with the buttons.

blocks.html: To turn a bigger unit into a smaller one, multiply by each step in turn. 2 T of wheat is 2 × 6 = 12 V. 1 V is 4 Z, so 2 T is 12 × 4 = 48 Z. To go the other way, divide: 30 V of oil is 30 ÷ 6 = 5 S. A quantity is written largest unit first: GRA 3 T 2 V 1 means 3 units, 2 T and 1 V of wheat.

Why such odd ratios, 10 then 6 then 4? Measures grow out of real containers and habits, not out of a plan. Many ancient systems mix factors like 6, 4, 3 and 30 because they divide evenly into halves, thirds and quarters, which helps when sharing out rations. Our own cups, pints and gallons, or feet and inches, are just as mixed.

Converting measures as if they were decimal. Each step has its own ratio: 1 unit = 10 T, 1 T = 6 V, 1 V = 4 Z for dry goods. Check: after converting, convert back; if 3 T came out as 30 V, multiply back by the step (30 ÷ 6 = 5, not 3) and you will see the error.

blocks.html: Clay records come in several shapes, and the shape tells you what kind of record it is. You saw in Clay, Fire and Survival that tablets were working notes. Here are the main formats a reader meets.

Page-shaped tablets hold lists; narrow "palm-leaf" tablets hold a single entry about one transaction; clay labels were pressed onto baskets of tablets; sealings carry a seal impression and sometimes a word; and some words were painted on jars before firing.

blocks.html: Why the different shapes? Each fits a step of the bookkeeping. A scribe in the field or the storeroom wrote one transaction on a leaf. Back in the office, leaves were sorted into baskets with labels, and summaries were written on pages. So the format tells you where a record sits in the process, from a first note to a summary.

Picturing all tablets as big pages of text. Many are narrow "palm leaves" with a single line about one transaction. Check: when you see a leaf-shaped tablet, expect one entry, often a name, a logogram and a number; when you see a page, expect a list.

Not every record is a tablet. Large stirrup jars, used to ship oil and wine, sometimes carry painted Linear B words, often a name or a place. Many were found at Thebes, and analysis of their clay suggests that many of them were made on Crete. They show that writing traveled with goods between Crete and the mainland.

blocks.title: Which format?
blocks.q: A record names one shepherd, his place, the sheep logogram and a number. Which format is most likely?
steps: One transaction, one line.

blocks.title: Which format?
blocks.q: A record lists twenty groups of women workers with their rations, and a total at the bottom. Which format?
steps: Many lines and a total: a list.

blocks.html: The tablets of Pages, Leaves and Labels were not written by everyone. Specialists can tell one writer from another by the way they drew the signs, the way a teacher can recognize a student's handwriting. Each writer is called a "hand".
Each scribe's handwriting can be recognized and numbered. Scholars count about 66 hands at Knossos and 45 at Pylos. Writing seems to have been the work of a small group of palace scribes.

No scribe signed a tablet. Instead, scholars compare details: how a sign is drawn (one stroke or two, a loop or an angle), how big the signs are, how lines are spaced, which spelling a writer prefers. Emmett Bennett pioneered this study at Pylos. Each hand gets a number, and with it a pattern appears: one hand writes about sheep, another about bronze, another about land.

blocks.html: Why does it matter who wrote a tablet? Hands let scholars put scattered tablets back together, group records by office and see how the palace divided its work. If one hand wrote all the records about perfumed oil, that suggests one office, or one official, handled the oil business. Hands turn a heap of tablets into an organization.

Imagining many people could write. With only a few dozen hands at each palace, writing seems to have been a specialist palace skill, not something ordinary people did. Check: no Linear B letters or private notes have been found; the texts are palace business.

Hands also help with broken tablets. Many tablets reached museums in pieces. When two fragments share a hand, a subject and a clay color, they may be parts of one tablet, and scholars have joined many fragments this way. Each join can complete a word or a total that was missing.

blocks.q: Pylos has about 1,000 tablets and about 45 hands. On average, about how many tablets per hand is that?
steps: 1,000 ÷ 45 is a little over 22.
blocks.a: About 22 tablets per hand (in fact some hands wrote far more than others).

blocks.title: What a hand tells
blocks.q: Every tablet about chariot wheels at a palace is in the same hand. What might that suggest?
steps: One writer handled one subject.
blocks.a: One scribe, or one office, was in charge of the chariot records.

blocks.html: You now have every piece: the signs (The Five Vowel Signs to Special Signs), the spelling rules (Clusters and Empty Vowels), the logograms (Logograms) and the numbers (Aegean Numbers). Time to read a tablet line the way a specialist does.

Most lines follow one pattern: a word or name, then a logogram, then a number. A short stroke, the word divider, separates spelled words. Find the divider, the logogram and the number first; then read the word.

blocks.html: Why start from the end? Because the number and the logogram can be read even when the word cannot. If the word is a name you have never seen, you still know what and how many. Scholars read damaged tablets this way: the logogram and number often survive when part of the word is broken.

Reading straight through and turning the logogram into a syllable, as if 𐀂𐀦 𐂃 were a three-syllable word. Find the word divider, the logogram and the number first, then read the word. Check: a logogram is never joined to the signs before it; it stands alone before the number.

blocks.html: With the spelling rules of Missing Consonants and Diphthongs and Glides you can see through a Linear B spelling to the Greek word behind it. Many of those words are still recognizable in later Greek, some even in English.

Mycenaean is Greek: many of its words live on in later Greek. ti-ri-po is tripous (tripod), di-pa is depas (cup), e-ra-wo is elaion (olive oil), wa-na-ka is anax (lord). Some words changed sound over the centuries: the w of wanax and woinos was lost.

blocks.html: Greek kept changing after the palaces fell. The w sound disappeared from most dialects, so wanax became anax and woinos became oinos. The kʷ and gʷ sounds written with q turned into p, b or t: gʷasileus (qa-si-re-u) became basileus. Homer's poems, written down centuries later, still show traces of the lost w in their rhythm, which scholars had suspected before the tablets were read.

blocks.html: Why are these words such strong evidence that the decipherment is right? Because they arrive with their sound changes exactly where Greek scholars had predicted. Linguists had reconstructed a w in "wine" and "lord", and a kʷ in "horse", from comparisons with other languages, long before 1952. The tablets, read with Ventris's values, showed those very sounds.

Thinking Mycenaean is a different language from Greek. It is Greek, about 500 years older than Homer's poems were written down, the way Chaucer's English is older English. Some words changed sound (wanax became anax). Check: strip the spelling rules away and look for a Greek word; if it is there, with an older sound or two, you are reading Mycenaean Greek.

blocks.html: In Mycenaean Words and Their Descendants you saw words. Greek, like Latin, changes the ending of a noun to show its job in the sentence: subject, owner, receiver and so on. These endings are the "cases". The spelling rules hide many endings, but some show through clearly, and they look older than Classical Greek.

Some endings show through the spelling: -o-jo for the genitive of o-stems (te-o-jo, "of the god"), -e and -i for datives (di-we, "to Zeus"), and -pi for an instrumental plural (Greek -phi). There is also a dual, a form for exactly two: ti-ri-po-de, "two tripods".

blocks.html: The genitive -oio (written -o-jo) became -ou in Classical Greek, but Homer still uses -oio, an echo of the older language that the tablets show in everyday use. The instrumental plural -phi (written -pi, since ph uses the p signs) had nearly disappeared by Classical times, though Homer keeps a few old phrases with it. The dual, for pairs, was still common in Mycenaean and faded later.

Why do some endings show and others hide? Because of the spelling rules. An ending of vowels, like -oio or -e, can be written in open syllables. An ending with a final consonant, like the -s of the nominative or the -n of the accusative, is dropped. So te-o could be theos (subject) or theon (object); the spelling cannot tell, and the reader must use context.

Endings are what Alice Kober caught in Alice Kober's Triplets. Her sets of three forms were words in different cases and genders, and the signs that changed at the end were case endings. When Ventris read the values, those endings turned out to be Greek ones, which was part of the proof.

Expecting the endings of Classical Greek. Mycenaean has older endings, like genitive -oio (written -o-jo), that Homer still uses. Check: an o-stem word ending in -o-jo is the genitive, "of …", not a new word.

blocks.html: Place names broke the code (The Breakthrough: Cretan Place Names), and they keep teaching us. The tablets name the towns, districts and harbors each palace ran. Read through the spelling rules of Mycenaean Words and Their Descendants, many match places known from later Greek.
ko-no-so (Knossos), pa-i-to (Phaistos), a-mi-ni-so (Amnisos), ku-do-ni-ja (Kydonia, modern Chania), pu-ro (Pylos) and te-qa (Thebes) are named on the tablets.

blocks.html: Why do place names last so long? People keep calling a town what their parents called it, even when rulers and languages change. Knossos, Phaistos and Pylos kept their names for thousands of years. That is why a name in a Bronze Age list can be matched with a name in a later Greek writer, and why decipherers love place names.

Expecting the place names to look like their modern spellings. Read them through the spelling rules: ko-no-so loses its double s, and te-qa uses q for Thebes' old kʷ-type sound. Check: undo the rules step by step (add back the final s, read r as l, p as ph) before you compare.

Not every name can be found on a map. The Pylos tablets name more than a dozen districts of the kingdom, and the Knossos tablets name many places across Crete. Some match later names; many do not, because the towns were abandoned or renamed. Scholars place them roughly by the goods they send and the other places listed with them.

Among the words you can now read (Endings You Can See) are names that every reader of Greek myths knows. The tablets record offerings to gods, and many of those gods are the Olympians of later Greece, named centuries before Homer.
The tablets name po-se-da-o (Poseidon), di-we and di-wo (Zeus, "to Zeus", "of Zeus"), e-ra (Hera), di-wo-nu-so (Dionysus), e-ma-a2 (Hermes) and a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja (Mistress Athena), among others.
