blocks.html: The gods turn up at several palaces: Zeus, Hera and Poseidon at Pylos; Mistress Athena and others at Knossos; Dionysus at Chania and Pylos. Some offering lists are dated by month, so the tablets also tell us a little about the religious year, though not what the gods were believed to do.

Why are we confident these are gods, not people with the same names? The context: these names receive offerings of oil, honey, gold vessels or animals, often at named shrines, in lists alongside words like te-o (god) and po-ti-ni-ja (lady). And the names match later Greek gods through the regular spelling rules.

Assuming the Olympians were invented later, in Homer's time or after. Several are named on the tablets, though we know little of the myths told about them then; the tablets give names and offerings, not stories. Check: separate what the tablets show (a name and an offering) from what later myths add (family stories, adventures).

blocks.html: The reading of e-ma-a2 as Hermes (e-ma-ha) is widely accepted, but the a2 sign makes the exact form a little uncertain. A few other names, like Drimios, have no later Greek match at all.
You can read a tablet line (Reading a Tablet Line). Now step back and look at thousands of them together. What were the palaces keeping track of, and what does that tell us about how they worked?

The tablets track what came into the palace and what went out: flocks and wool, oil and perfume, grain and rations for workers, bronze for smiths, chariots and armor, land, and offerings to the gods. They are accounts, and their value is in the patterns across thousands of entries.

blocks.html: Scholars often describe the palace economy as redistributive: goods flowed into the palace as taxes or dues and flowed out again as rations, raw materials for craftsmen and offerings. The tablets show this in action. A shepherd owes so many sheep; a group of women is given so much wheat and figs; a smith receives so much bronze and is expected to return finished work. The palaces did not control everything, though; many activities, such as most pottery making, barely appear in the records.

Why are patterns more valuable than any single tablet? One tablet says "at Phaistos: rams, 100". Thousands of tablets like it let scholars map where the flocks were, how big they were, how much wool was expected and how close each shepherd came. Single lines are dull; together they show a whole economy at work.

Expecting stories or letters. The tablets are accounts, with lists of names, things and numbers. Check: if you are looking for "what happened" in a tablet, ask instead "what was counted, by whom, and where?"

blocks.html: The palace accounts of The Palace Economy also name the people at the top. Their titles, read with the spelling rules of Mycenaean Words and Their Descendants, give us a glimpse of how a Mycenaean state was run.

The wa-na-ka (wanax) ruled the palace state; the ra-wa-ke-ta (lawagetas) ranked next; a qa-si-re-u (later basileus, "king") was a lesser local official. The title wanax survives in Homer as anax, "lord".

items: The wanax stood at the head of the state, with religious and economic roles. Craftsmen are sometimes described as working for him.
The lawagetas, "leader of the people" (from lawos, people, and agō, I lead), ranked second. His exact duties are debated; some think they were military, others religious or administrative.
The e-qe-ta (hekʷetai, "followers") were officials or companions attached to the palace.
The qa-si-re-u (gʷasileus) was a local official, in charge of a group of bronzesmiths for example, far below the wanax.

blocks.html: Notice what the titles do not tell us: the names of the men who held them. The tablets speak of "the wanax" as an office, the way a modern form says "the mayor". So we know a Mycenaean state had a ruler and a second-in-command, but not, for certain, who any particular wanax of Pylos or Knossos was.

Why did a minor title become the word for "king"? When the palaces fell (The End of the Palaces), the wanax and his court vanished. The local leaders survived, and with no palace above them, they became the most important men around. Their title, basileus, rose with them. By Homer's time and in Classical Greek, basileus meant king, while anax lived on mainly in poetry and for gods.

Reading qa-si-re-u as "king". In the tablets the basileus was a minor official; the word rose in status only after the palaces fell. Check: in a Linear B text, the ruler is the wa-na-ka; translate qa-si-re-u as "chief" or "official".

blocks.html: In Gods on the Tablets you met the gods by name. The same tablets tell what was given to them, where and sometimes when. Some of these records are easy to read; one of them is among the most debated texts in the whole archive.

Tablets list offerings of oil, honey, grain, animals and gold vessels to gods. Pylos tablet Tn 316 records gold vessels, and men and women, brought to Zeus, Hera and others. Some scholars read those people as human offerings; others as servants given to the gods' service. The text does not settle it.

blocks.html: Most religious tablets are plain lists. Pylos sends perfumed oil to Poseidon and to goddesses called Potnia. A Knossos tablet sends a jar of honey (me-ri) to Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, at Amnisos. Others send wheat, wine or animals to shrines, sometimes dated by month. They show a calendar of festivals run partly through the palace.

Tn 316 is a page-shaped tablet written on both sides. It lists shrines and gods, and for each a gold vessel and, often, a man or a woman. The extract above shows three entries. The question is what the people were for. One reading: they were sacrificed, perhaps in an emergency as the palace faced its end. Another: they were given to the god as servants of the shrine, as later temples had temple servants. A few have suggested other readings.

blocks.html: Why can't the tablet settle it? Because it is an account, not a description. It says what went where, with logograms for "man" and "woman" and numbers; it gives no verb for what happened to them. Any reading must add information from outside the tablet, so scholars still disagree.

Taking one reading of a hard tablet as fact. Some scholars read Tn 316's people as human offerings; others as servants given to the gods' service. Check: when a book says "the Mycenaeans sacrificed humans at Pylos", ask what the tablet actually says: a god's name, a gold bowl, VIR 1.

blocks.html: After The Palace Economy you know what the tablets do say: who owed what, who got what, where and how much. It is just as important to know what they do not say, because the gap is where many popular mistakes begin.

No poems, laws, letters or histories survive in Linear B. The tablets record one season's palace business. They name no war, no Agamemnon and no Trojan War, and much about these people remains unknown.

blocks.html: Three reasons. First, Linear B was a palace bookkeeping tool, used by a few scribes for accounts (Scribes and Their Hands). Second, clay survived only where fire baked it, so we have the files of the last months, not the long-term records (Clay, Fire and Survival). Third, any longer texts may have been written on materials such as wood or leather, if they existed at all; none has survived, so we cannot know.

Why does the silence matter? Because it limits what the tablets can prove. They cannot confirm or deny Homer's Trojan War: they do not mention it. They cannot tell us what the Mycenaeans thought, only what they counted. A claim that "the tablets show" a story or a belief should make you check which tablet, and what it actually says.

Expecting the tablets to confirm Homer or tell of the Trojan War. They name no war, no Agamemnon and no history at all. Check: Homer's heroes are absent from the tablets as people. A few names that match Homeric heroes (such as Achilles, as a name) turn up for ordinary people, which shows the names were in use, not that the heroes lived.

blocks.html: Now we turn to the older script, the one the Minoans of The Minoans of Crete used and the Mycenaeans borrowed (A Family of Aegean Scripts). Linear A has been known since Evans's time, and it is still unread. Before asking why, look at what there is to read.

Linear A is the Minoan script, used from about 1800 to 1450 BC. About 1,400 inscriptions survive, with about 7,400 signs in all, most of them short lists from Hagia Triada, Zakros, Chania and Phaistos.

blocks.html: Why does the size of the corpus matter so much? Compare: about 7,400 signs of Linear A, against tens of thousands of words of Linear B. Every pattern a decipherer finds must be seen many times to be trusted. With little text, and much of it lists of names and numbers, there are few patterns to test.

Thinking Linear A is a large body of texts. It is small: about 7,400 signs in all, mostly short lists, many damaged. Check: the whole corpus would fit in a few pages of a book, while the Linear B archives fill large volumes.

blocks.html: Look at Linear A and Linear B side by side and something jumps out: many signs have nearly the same shapes. That is no accident; Linear B was adapted from Linear A (A Family of Aegean Scripts). It also gives us a way to sound out Linear A, with a warning label attached. (Recall the special signs of Special Signs; some of them are shared too.)

Many Linear A signs look like Linear B signs, so scholars read them with the Linear B values by convention. This is a working guess about sounds: likely for many signs, but not proved, and it does not tell us the language.

blocks.html: Because there is some evidence that many carried over. Place names give the best: the Linear A word read pa-i-to with the borrowed values is the same as Linear B pa-i-to, Phaistos, and Hagia Triada, where it appears, is next to Phaistos. Other words, such as su-ki-ri-ta and se-to-i-ja, appear in both scripts as names of Cretan places. If the values were wrong, such matches would be unlikely.

blocks.html: Why is this still only a convention? The place names show that some values carried over, but not all. The Mycenaeans may have changed some values to suit Greek, as they added and dropped signs. And knowing sounds is not knowing a language: we can say ku-ro aloud, more or less, without knowing what language it is. The convention lets scholars talk about words and compare them; it does not read them.

Treating Linear A sound values as known. They are borrowed from Linear B on the assumption that the sounds carried over with the shapes, which is likely for many signs but not proved. Check: always say "read by convention as ku-ro", and never use a Linear A reading as proof of a meaning.

blocks.html: Linear A uses the same counting marks you learned in Aegean Numbers: strokes, bars, circles and rayed circles. So you can read every whole number on a Linear A tablet today. But Linear A also has something Linear B lacks: signs for fractions.

Linear A counts with the same decimal marks as Linear B and also has fraction signs, named by letters. J as one half is widely accepted; values for the others (E 1/4, F 1/8, K 1/10, B 1/5, D 1/6) are proposals, and H, A and L are uncertain or unknown.

When a list with fractions adds up only if J is one half, that is evidence for J. Scholars work through many lists this way. J fits again and again; the other values fit some lists and are disputed in others. Signs can also combine: JE is read as 3/4, if E is 1/4.

Rarer signs appear in fewer lists, often damaged, so several values might fit, or none fits perfectly. A value proved by one list could be a coincidence; a value that works in dozens is not.

The word read ku-ro stands before a number that equals the sum of the list above it, so it is widely accepted to mean "total". The word read ki-ro also recurs in lists before numbers; its meaning is uncertain.

blocks.html: Other words are less clear. po-to-ku-ro seems to sum several totals and is often taken as a "grand total", less securely. ki-ro also stands before numbers in lists; some suggest it marks an amount owed or missing, but there is no agreement.

Why is this meaning trusted when nothing else in Linear A is? Because it does not depend on knowing the language. Arithmetic is the same in every language. A word that always stands before the sum of a list does the job of "total" whatever it sounds like. It is a meaning found by function, the same way you could tell what "Gesamt" does on a German receipt without knowing German.

Thinking that knowing ku-ro means we can read Linear A. We know what the word does from the arithmetic, not what language it belongs to. Check: ku-ro does not even prove the sounds; "ku-ro" is its conventional reading, and its meaning would be the same if the signs were said quite differently.

blocks.html: Not all of Linear A is bookkeeping. On stone offering tables from Cretan sanctuaries, carved texts repeat the same words in the same order. Scholars call this the libation formula. It is one of the most studied puzzles in the script, and a lesson in what can and cannot be said. You will need the conventional readings of Signs Shared with Linear B.

Stone offering tables from sanctuaries repeat a set of words, such as a-sa-sa-ra-me (also ja-sa-sa-ra-me), i-pi-na-ma and si-ru-te. They are recognized because they recur in the same order; their meanings are unknown.

That is the same kind of evidence Alice Kober used for Linear B (Alice Kober's Triplets). It can tell us that a-sa-sa-ra-me and ja-sa-sa-ra-me are forms of one word, without telling us what that word means.

blocks.html: You have seen what Linear A offers (Ku-ro, the Total, The Libation Formula). Linear B was cracked in 1952; Linear A, which uses many of the same signs, still resists. The difference is not cleverness. It is evidence.

Linear A cannot be read yet because the texts are few and short, the Minoan language matches no known language, and there is no bilingual text, like the Rosetta Stone, giving the same words in a known script.

blocks.html: Why can't the borrowed values simply read Linear A? They give sounds, roughly, but sounds in an unknown language are just syllables. Reading means knowing what words mean and how they fit together. With Linear B the values led straight into Greek, a known language. With Linear A they lead into a language nobody knows, so there is nothing to recognize.

Thinking more cleverness is all it takes. Without more texts, a related known language or a bilingual, there is not enough to test a reading. Check: ask what new evidence a claimed decipherment uses. If none, it is choosing among many possible guesses that the small corpus cannot rule out.
New finds could change this. A large new archive, or a bilingual inscription, would give scholars much more to work with. Until then, Linear A remains, in the words of many specialists, undeciphered.

blocks.html: Every few years someone announces that they have deciphered Linear A. The news spreads, and then, usually quietly, specialists explain why they are not convinced. After Why Linear A Can't Be Read Yet you can see why such claims are hard to make good. This lesson gives you the tools to judge one yourself, using the one decipherment that did succeed, Linear B (The Tripod Tablet Confirms It), as the model.

A good decipherment makes testable predictions, reads the whole corpus the same way, fits place names and new finds, and convinces specialists who check it. Claims to read Linear A appear every few years; none has met these tests or been accepted.

blocks.html: Why are a few matching words not enough? Because chance produces matches. Linear A has hundreds of short words, and the world has thousands of languages with millions of words. Allow some freedom in sounds and meanings, and a handful of "hits" will turn up for almost any language. A real decipherment is shown by what it does with all the rest, and above all by texts it had not seen.

Check: ask whether the claim uses fixed values, reads the whole corpus, makes a prediction that came true, and has convinced independent experts.
This course does not discuss particular claims or the people who made them. The tests above apply to any claim, and you can use them on the next one you read about.

Linear A and Linear B share many sign shapes and the same numbers, but they write different languages: Linear B writes Greek, Linear A an unknown language. Linear B could be read because it had a known language, a large corpus and good tests; Linear A has none of these yet.

blocks.html: Why do the shared signs not make Linear A readable? Shapes can be borrowed while languages differ. The Latin alphabet writes English, French and Turkish; knowing the letters lets you sound out a Turkish sentence but not understand it. Linear A is in the same position, except that its sounds are themselves only a convention.

Thinking Linear A and Linear B are two languages written the same way, or the same language. They share signs, but Linear B writes Greek and Linear A an unknown language. blocks.q: A tablet from Pylos lists ti-ri-po with the tripod sign. Which script is it in?
steps: Pylos is a mainland palace.
ti-ri-po is a Greek word.

blocks.title: Which script?
blocks.q: A stone offering table from a Cretan peak sanctuary carries the words a-sa-sa-ra-me and i-pi-na-ma. Which script?
steps: Stone libation tables with this formula belong to Minoan Crete.
These are words of the libation formula, read by convention.
